questions.q: Why must gold.daily_sales_summary and gold.category_breakdown always reconcile with each other?
options: Both are built from the same silver.sales_clean rows, just grouped at a different level of detail
They are unrelated tables that happen to coincidentally agree
They both read directly from bronze.sales_raw, bypassing Silver entirely
Power BI automatically keeps them in sync
questions.explain: Both Gold tables derive from the exact same Silver rows; daily_sales_summary collapses category, category_breakdown keeps it. Same source, different grain.

questions.q: To compare the two Gold tables, how must gold.category_breakdown be aggregated before joining?
options: Grouped by store_id and sale_date, summing total_sales across all categories
Grouped by category only, ignoring store_id
Filtered to a single category and compared row-for-row
Left exactly as-is, since it already matches the other table's grain
questions.explain: Rolling category_breakdown back up to the store_id/sale_date grain (summing total_sales across category) is what makes it comparable to daily_sales_summary.

questions.q: Why does the reconciliation query check ABS(diff) > 0.01 instead of an exact inequality?
options: To make the query run faster
Because the business accepts being off by up to a dollar
Because Delta Lake rounds all currency columns to the nearest cent automatically
To absorb tiny floating-point/decimal rounding noise without masking a real discrepancy
questions.explain: The one-cent tolerance exists only to absorb rounding noise from summing currency at different grouping levels — not to hide genuinely wrong numbers.

questions.q: What should the discrepancy report return when run against the pipeline as it stands in this lesson?
options: One row per store, showing a small expected difference
Every row in gold.daily_sales_summary, for comparison
An error, because the two tables have incompatible schemas
Zero rows — both Gold tables currently reconcile cleanly
questions.explain: At this point in the story both Gold tables were built correctly from the same incremental Silver layer, so the query should come back clean with zero discrepancy rows.

questions.q: Why does the lesson tell you to keep this exact query instead of discarding it after this check?
options: Because it becomes the diagnostic tool you reuse later in the course when something actually breaks
Because it's needed to build gold.category_breakdown in the first place
Because Power BI requires it to be saved as a stored procedure
Because the query must run nightly to populate bronze.sales_raw
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly foreshadows that this same reconciliation query gets run again, for real, later in the course when the two tables actually stop agreeing.
